query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In initially single-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs), brittle behavior under service conditions emerges primarily when local chemical ordering or clustering at grain boundaries induces the formation of embrittling phases or disrupts the entropy-stabilized matrix, rather than from conventional grain-boundary segregation or precipitation seen in traditional alloys. The high configurational entropy suppresses rapid grain coarsening and intermetallic precipitation, but under certain thermal or mechanical loading, local ordering can reduce entropy locally and trigger brittle grain-boundary features.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., FCC or BCC HEA, homogenized and solution-treated, with fine grains and no detectable grain-boundary precipitation or segregation)
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal exposure (e.g., annealing at intermediate temperatures) or mechanical loading (e.g., cyclic deformation) to induce possible local ordering or clustering at grain boundaries without changing overall phase composition.
generation.conditions: Temperatures and stresses relevant to engineering service (e.g., 400–800°C for thermal exposure, or room temperature to cryogenic for mechanical loading); maintain alloy composition and avoid external contamination.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering or clustering at grain boundaries, leading to reduced local entropy and possible formation of embrittling features (e.g., short-range ordered regions, nano-scale precipitates, or depleted zones)
generation.mechanism: Local reduction in configurational entropy at grain boundaries enables the emergence of brittle features, which act as crack initiation sites and reduce toughness, even in the absence of conventional grain-boundary precipitation or segregation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial single-phase HEA baseline, toughness (e.g., Charpy impact energy or fracture toughness) will decrease after exposure to conditions that promote local ordering or clustering, but not after conditions that only promote conventional grain-boundary segregation or precipitation. The drop in toughness will be less severe than in conventional alloys under similar treatments, but measurable and correlated with evidence of local ordering at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: Single-phase HEA with high toughness and no evidence of grain-boundary embrittlement or precipitation; conventional alloy baseline would show rapid toughness loss with grain-boundary precipitation.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis holds for compositionally complex, entropy-stabilized alloys with initially single-phase microstructure; fails if the alloy is not entropy-stabilized or if conventional precipitation dominates. Service boundaries: intermediate temperatures, cyclic loading, or environments that promote local ordering.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of toughness loss and exact nature of local ordering/clustering are uncertain due to lack of direct evidence; mechanism inferred from analogy and prior reports on HEA stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase HEA samples: one subjected to thermal/mechanical treatments known to induce local ordering at grain boundaries (but not conventional precipitation), and one subjected to treatments that induce conventional grain-boundary segregation/precipitation. Compare toughness (e.g., Charpy impact energy, fracture toughness) and microstructural features (using atom probe tomography, TEM, and grain-boundary analysis).
measurements: atom probe tomography of grain boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If toughness loss in HEAs correlates only with conventional grain-boundary precipitation/segregation and not with local ordering/clustering, or if no measurable toughness loss occurs after local ordering/clustering, the hypothesis is falsified.
